figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: The Edge0 system. Expert weights stay on SSD as int4 per-layer stacked safetensors and are mmap-streamed on demand into a bounded streaming pool (OS page cache, LRU, staged fixed-slot double buffer). A frozen int4 decoder stack computes with a parallel, unmerged recovery LoRA branch, $y=W_{\mathrm{int4}}(x)+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}\,BA\,x$, combined at a sum node. The prerouter head owned by layer $N$ predicts layer $N{+}1$’s routing one token ahead (red path, “prediction is the routing”), so the SSD reads that fill the staged slots overlap the forward pass; the decode timeline at the bottom shows the predicted read of token $t{+}1$ running concurrently with the compute of token $t$.
figures.headline: Expert weights stream from SSD into a bounded pool, and a prerouter predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 shows the system architecture and the decode-time dataflow.
Layer $N{+}1$ consumes the prediction made one token earlier; the SSD read that fills its slots overlaps the current forward pass (Figure 1).

figures.caption: The advantage of the prerouter, on a 16 GB MacBook M2 with an 18.4 GiB checkpoint that does not fit. (a) Decode throughput: pure on-demand streaming against every staged layer prefetching its next token’s experts. (b) The same cold pages read in fewer, larger loads, with the cold fraction of each load printed above its bar; per-load cost follows $1.17\,\mathrm{ms}+1.33\,\mathrm{ms}\times$cold. figures.headline: Prerouter prefetching raises decode throughput at each routing width tested, reading cold pages in fewer, larger loads.
citing_sentences: 3) on a MacBook M2 with 16 GB of unified memory holding the release directory (18.4 GiB: a 19.5 GB int4 base plus 0.2 GB of adapter and prerouter heads), a machine on which the weights do not fit, so every step faults experts back in from the SSD, with mlx 0.30.4–0.30.6 spanning the campaigns [2].
The cost being removed is serialized load latency, and removing it is what the predictor buys (Figure 3a).
The same cold pages then arrive in fewer, larger loads: 1.40 MiB per load at 90% cold, against 0.32 MiB per load at 20% cold for on-demand streaming (Figure 3b, Table 4).

abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on consumer hardware is bounded by weight memory: a 35B-class model is 19.5 GB at 4-bit, and sparsity shrinks the compute per token, not the bytes that must be held. Naive offloading to SSD does not help on its own, because layer $N{+}1$’s experts must be chosen before layer $N$’s output exists, so the reads cannot start early enough to hide behind compute. We present Edge0, a streaming MoE inference engine that closes the gap with a prerouter: a per-layer head predicts the next layer’s routing one token ahead, and the prediction is consumed as the routing itself, so the staged expert set equals the routed set and nothing is dropped. An unmerged recovery LoRA, trained on the student path, pays back the quality lost to int4 quantization and routing replacement. On a single 24 GB machine, Edge0 serves a 35B MoE at ${\approx}$20 tok/s inside 3 GiB of peak active memory, within a few points of its fp16 teacher on average across five public benchmarks. An 8B tier runs on the same framework, and the framework, checkpoints, and adapters are open source.

sections.body: The introduction says a 35B-class MoE at 4-bit needs nineteen and a half gigabytes of weights, and that sparsity cuts compute per token but not stored bytes. Offloading to SSD alone stalls because layer N+1's experts depend on layer N's output. Edge0 streams expert weights from SSD on demand and uses a per-layer prerouter that predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, so reads overlap the forward pass. The prediction is used as the routing, so no staged expert is dropped. An unmerged recovery LoRA, trained on the student path, recovers quality lost to int4 quantization and routing replacement. The listed contributions report +80 to +84% decode from prediction-as-routing on a machine where the checkpoint does not fit.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Storing 35B-class MoE weights on a 24 GB machine is the bottleneck, so Edge0 keeps experts on SSD and streams them.

sections.body: The background covers two MoE routing families, softmax-top-k and sigmoid-group, both implemented verbatim and reused for prerouter training. It contrasts pre-gated MoE, which selects the next block's experts within the same token, with Edge0's one-token lead. Quantization work made 4-bit the practical post-training working point, and Edge0 accepts the loss and recovers most of it by distillation. Offloading systems such as `--cpu-moe`, PowerInfer, Mixtral-offloading, MoE-Infinity and FlexGen are listed. The section states that they move the footprint rather than shrink it, and that disk-resident weights are fetched without knowing which experts the next step needs.
sections.heading: Background and Related Work
sections.headline: Prior offloading moves the weight footprint rather than shrinking it, and pre-gating schedules next-block experts too late for a streaming engine.

sections.body: A 40-layer, 256-expert model holds 453 MB of expert weights per layer at int4, so routed experts take 16.9 GiB of a 19.5 GB checkpoint. Edge0 mmaps the quantized expert safetensors and reads byte ranges on demand, so peak memory tracks the active set. Four executor paths (exact, staged, hot, whole-layer) compute the same quantized expert function and are checked element-wise against the dequantized reference, with relative L2 error under 1% and a measured residual of about 0.24%. On a 24 GB Mac mini M4 Pro, a resident server holding 18.2 GiB decodes at 3.9 tok/s, while the K=4 profile decodes at 20.4 tok/s in 2.9 GiB. The recovery LoRA stays unmerged; merging it would keep 34% of its effect on an attention projection and 2% on a dense projection.
sections.heading: System Design
sections.headline: A 40-layer MoE needs 16.9 GiB of routed experts, so Edge0 mmaps them from SSD across four executor paths.

sections.body: All three phases train on the dequantized bf16 reconstruction of the 4-bit checkpoint, with the base frozen. Phase 1 distills the prerouter heads to imitate the next layer's true router. Phase 2 trains a LoRA on attention, linear-attention and shared-expert projections, not routed experts, with prerouting active, over roughly two million rows of teacher text. Without this phase, distillation-only checkpoints with student routing produced repetitive, collapsed text. Phase 3 runs on-policy reverse-KL distillation on the student's own generations over roughly 200k rows, one tenth of the Phase 2 corpus. Retraining for a narrower routing width is a file swap: the 35B tier ships at K=4 instead of K=8, and in a same-session A/B on a 16 GB machine narrowing moved decode from 3.3 to 6.4 tok/s.
sections.heading: Training
sections.headline: Three training phases make the model work under replaced routing: head distillation, fine-tuning on the student path, and on-policy distillation.

sections.body: Two public tiers are measured on a 24 GB Mac mini M4 Pro: the 35B model at K=4 (20.4 tok/s, 2.9 GiB peak) and an 8B model (28.0 tok/s, 1.5 GiB peak). Quality is scored with OpenCompass on five benchmarks against each fp16 base under identical settings; mean per-benchmark gaps are 3.9 points for the 35B tier and 2.8 for the 8B. The prerouter A/B runs on a 16 GB MacBook M2 with an 18.4 GiB checkpoint, where it raises decode by +80 to +84% across the tested widths by moving expert-load latency off the critical path. Runs are same-session, rotated and reported as medians; single-shot runs vary by ±40%, so no cross-session number is used as evidence.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Both tiers average within a few points of fp16 bases, and the prerouter adds +80 to +84% decode where weights do not fit.

sections.body: Edge0 serves one request at a time, FIFO-serialized, and batching is not modeled. Streaming decode is CPU-side: 44 ms per step of graph building in the 40-layer forward is the floor, and storage-side changes do not move it. Prerouter gains shrink with hot caches or fast storage and are bounded by reuse, since adjacent tokens agree on only about a quarter of a layer's experts. Quality loss concentrates in long-chain reasoning: 6.1 points on AIME for the 35B tier and 10.0 for the 8B tier, with every other 8B benchmark within 6.7 points and MMLU-Pro 4.3 points in the student's favour. Only the MLX backend is implemented; the CUDA slot is architecture, not code.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Decode has a 44 ms per-step floor from graph building, quality loss concentrates in long-chain reasoning, and one backend exists.

sections.body: The conclusion says the weights half of the memory wall is a storage placement decision, and Edge0 places experts on SSD. A trained prerouter predicts routing one token ahead so loads hide under compute, prediction is the routing so nothing is dropped, and a distilled, unmerged LoRA covers the 4-bit quality loss. The 35B-class MoE runs at 20 tok/s inside 3 GiB on a 24 GB desktop; the 8B hybrid runs at 28 tok/s inside 1.5 GiB. Both are described as within a few points of their fp16 teachers. The framework, checkpoints, and adapters are released under Apache-2.0.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: A 35B MoE runs at 20 tok/s in 3 GiB on a 24 GB desktop, with framework, checkpoints, and adapters open source.

sections.body: The appendix gives the two routing functions, extracted verbatim from the vendored models and shared by the resident, streaming and prerouter paths; parity tests pin them bit-identical. Softmax-top-k takes the softmax of the logits, selects the top K, and renormalizes the selected weights. Sigmoid-group applies sigmoid scores, keeps the best G of n groups ranked by their top-two score sums, selects the top K within survivors, and scales raw sigmoid weights by s. The 8B tier runs n=8, G=4, s=2.5, K=8. Appendix B reports that incremental stacking adds a further +34% decode in a separate A/B, and that native routing rises from 6.8 to 12.5 tok/s at K=8 in an earlier campaign whose rates are not comparable with Table 3.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives the softmax-top-k and sigmoid-group routing formulas and the incremental-stack assembly A/B results.
